title: The Yaksha's question
hookLine: a voice at a lake asks Yudhishthira what the greatest wonder is
carry: five afflictions, one root: seeing wrongly
tomorrow: ignorance — mistaking the passing for the permanent

cards: The five Pandava brothers are deep in the forest, exhausted and thirsty. Nakula finds a clear lake, and a voice calls out: answer my questions first, then drink. He drinks anyway, and falls.
Sahadeva, Arjuna and Bhima come looking, ignore the voice, and fall by the water too. Then Yudhishthira arrives, sees his brothers lying there, and does what none of them did. He listens.
The voice is a yaksha, a spirit of the lake, and it asks question after question.

teach.b: One of them: what is the greatest wonder? Yudhishthira answers: every day, creatures go to the house of death, and those who remain want to live forever. What could be more wonderful than that?

The yaksha turns out to be Dharma himself, Yudhishthira's divine father, and gives the brothers back their lives. Hold that answer up to Patanjali. Sutra 2.3: avidya asmita raga dvesha abhiniveshah kleshah.
Ignorance, I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging to life are the afflictions. Klesha means affliction, a cause of pain.

Abhinivesha, clinging to life, is last on the list, and sutra 2.9 says it's found even in the wise. That's the yaksha's wonder: everyone sees death, and lives as if it won't come for them. Under it are the others.

teach.h: PULL, PUSH, I-NESS, AND THE ROOT.
teach.b: Raga, the pull toward what pleased. Dvesha, the push away from what hurt. Asmita, the sense of a separate me who is pleased and hurt.

And first, avidya, ignorance: not a lack of facts, but seeing wrongly, taking what passes for what lasts. The next sutra calls ignorance the field the other four grow in. Here's the teaching, plainly.
For Patanjali the deepest root of human trouble isn't bad luck, and even misdeeds grow from something underneath. It's a mistake about what's real, which the mind then defends.

So the cure is seeing clearly, not only trying harder. This week walked toward it: many doors, a toddler's mouth, the archer's bird, Narada's words, Ramakrishna's last seed, Parvati's heat, and now the roots.

how: Hindus retell the yaksha's questions as a test of wisdom, and students of the Yoga Sutras learn the five kleshas as the root diagnosis of suffering; some teachers ask them to trace everyday reactions back to these roots in meditation and daily life.

o: seeing wrongly: taking the passing as lasting
a punishment for wrongs in a past life
simply not having read enough scripture

games.q: the lake and the roots: tap the pairs.
p: all die, yet all wish to live forever
clinging to life, even in the wise

s: the four brothers fell because they drank before answering
the voice said answer first; only Yudhishthira listened.
avidya means not knowing enough facts
it means seeing wrongly, taking what passes for what lasts.
the next sutra calls ignorance the field for the other four.

games.q: you snap at a friend over something small. Patanjali would want you to look where?
o: at the root: which affliction it grows from, and beneath it, ignorance.
games.why: 2.3 names five roots. a snap is often aversion, or wounded I-ness, and the next sutra says all of them grow from ignorance.

practice: As thoughts come, sort them gently into the five: wanting something is attraction, avoiding something is aversion, me and my image is I-ness, a flicker of fear about the future is clinging.
You don't need to find ignorance; it's said to be under all of them. Just notice, name, and return to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Avidya, ignorance, mistaking the passing for the lasting, the root of the five afflictions. Patanjali names it first, then I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging to life, all four growing in its field.

orig.note: Sanskrit kleśa: affliction, a cause of pain. Patanjali names five in 2.3.

carryVoice: Your line: five afflictions, one root: seeing wrongly. The yaksha's wonder is a good first place to look. That's the week.
